newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In - Of hackers, threat agents and grass huts.
newsitem.headline: Plugged In - Of hackers, threat agents and grass huts.

text.p: Are you worried that while you sleep, unseen forces are trying to compromise your computer network and make off with digital valuables?
If you are not, you should be.

A subterranean force, some operating with sect-like fervor, is constantly looking at ways of cracking a network that could contain your client list, your credit card number or just about anything else.
"It's both fascinating and frightening. There are just no secrets anymore," said Norm Inkster, the former head of Canada's Mounties and now a security expert for the consulting firm KPMG in Toronto.
To protect public and private networks, companies are racing to build bigger and better electronic "firewalls," around their systems to protect sensitive data.
Computer hackers, however, see the firewall as nothing more than a minor irritant on the way to freeing up information held hostage in an increasingly closed digital society.
Even while security continues to tighten, these hackers remain extremely nimble and a few steps ahead of some of the best minds managing corporate and private networks.
Michael Zboray, an analyst at the research firm Gartner Group, likens some network security efforts to installing a steel door on a grass hut: there are just so many ways to break in.

The now famous invaders of the CIA web page, who in September changed the site's greeting to "the Central Stupidity Agency" and inflicted other humorous changes, were a case in point of what fun hackers can wreak.

The CIA pulled the plug on its site after the break in and assured everyone no vital secrets were at stake because the Web home page (http://www.odci.gov/cia) was not connected to the mainframes where the real goodies were kept.

It was a major symbolic victory for the hacker forces because it brought into question the security of any system if the world's best known secret service could be breached in such a spectacular fashion.

If you have any doubt about the growing hordes of hackers, check out "Hacker's Pages" category on the Yahoo search engine (http://www.yahoo.com/Computers_and_Internet/Security_and_Encryp tion/Hacking/Hacker_s_Pages/). There you will find a staggering list of happy hacker home sites -- everything from Aaron WinterMute's Hacking Phun Philes to Ziggiey's Hack Hut for Macs -- "a hut where you can find Mac Hacks, links and anarchy."
The hacker purists disavow those who try to break into networks for profit or to vandalize. They believe they perform a public service by keeping information open and free for all.
But analyst Zboray told a recent Gartner Conference in Florida that "threat agents" -- as he called them -- can be divided into three groups: the curious, the glory seekers and the mercenaries.

He said true hackers seek glory (as in the case of the CIA invasion), while mercenaries attack any and all weak points for any "valuables" in a network. The curious appear amateurish, leaving their electronic fingerprints everywhere.

Experts believe thousands of attacks are made on networks each day but organizations cannot depend on local authorities anymore to protect them because too often an attack on a local network comes from offshore.
Security with the emphasis on the firewall will continue to get more complex and, in theory, eventually become a stronger form of defense against the sophisticated electronic interlopers.
But will all the efforts really make us secure?
"We can anticipate the same kind of constant attack on computers systems to continue," said Inkster. "We just have to keep working at it."
